name: Segmental maxillary osteotomy

card.summary: Orthognathic surgery that cuts the upper jaw into sections to reposition them, changing arch width, bite and the position of the front teeth and upper lip.
card.aka: Le Fort segmental, segmental Le Fort I osteotomy
card.note: Major surgery under general anaesthesia with a documented complication rate; done by oral and maxillofacial surgeons.

quick.overview:
A segmental maxillary osteotomy is a jaw operation in which the upper jaw is cut horizontally, as in a Le Fort I osteotomy, and then divided into two or more pieces that are moved independently. This lets surgeons widen a narrow upper arch, close an open bite or adjust the height of the front section, which changes how the teeth, smile and upper lip look.

It is an established procedure in orthognathic and cleft surgery, with case series, planning-accuracy studies and a few registered trials. It is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as part of hardmaxxing, the term for surgical approaches.
quick.how: Patients are typically planned jointly by an orthodontist and an oral and maxillofacial surgeon, with braces before and after the operation. Surgery is performed under general anaesthesia, with the segments fixed using small titanium plates. Three-dimensional computer planning is increasingly used.
quick.risks: A British series of 85 patients reported an overall complication rate of 27 percent, including tooth devitalisation, minor gum defects, plate removal and palatal fistula. As with other jaw surgery, recovery involves swelling and dietary restriction, and results depend on surgeon experience.

lead: Segmental maxillary osteotomy is a surgical technique in which the maxilla is cut and divided into segments, so that parts of the upper jaw can be moved in different directions.[1][2] It is a variation of the Le Fort I osteotomy, named for the French surgeon René Le Fort, who described three midface fracture patterns in the early 1900s.[3]

Surgeons use it to correct vertical and transverse maxillary deformities, such as anterior open bite and a narrow upper arch.[1] Appearance changes follow from the repositioned teeth and arch: a wider arch can fill out the smile and a repositioned front segment changes the display of the incisors and lip support.
A 2016 review describes segmentation between the lateral incisors and canines as a versatile approach, allowing control of intercanine width and incisor angulation.[2]

chain: Upper jaw is cut and divided into segments
Segments are moved to widen the arch or change height
Smile, tooth display and lip support change
angle.text: The operation repositions parts of the upper jaw to alter arch width, bite and front-tooth position. People considering hardmaxxing look at it for changes to the smile and midface.

paras: In a segmental Le Fort I osteotomy the upper jaw is separated horizontally and then divided so segments can move in the sagittal and vertical planes, and, with multiple segments, in the transverse plane.[2] Typical cut sites are between the lateral incisors and canines, between premolars and canines, or between incisors, and cuts may be bilateral, unilateral or asymmetric.[2]

Indications in a British series of 85 patients were anterior open bite (35%), transverse maxillary deficiency (28%), both together (33%) and anterior vertical maxillary excess (4%).[1] A 2019 series used segmental osteotomy with bone grafting to close wide alveolar clefts in six patients, and all clefts closed with no adverse effects observed.[4]

In the 85-patient series (mean age 23.3, treated 1995-2009), the overall complication rate was 27%: three patients (4%) had tooth devitalisation, three (4%) minor periodontal defects, one lost a tooth, eight (9%) had plates removed and two had persistent palatal fistula; no bone segment or teeth were lost.[1] A case report describes hyperbaric oxygen therapy used for a palatal oro-nasal fistula after the procedure.[5]

A 2020 study measured how accurately computer-assisted three-dimensional planning translates to segmental maxillary surgery using cone-beam CT scans.[6] A related line of research examines patient-specific implants in virtually planned segmental operations.[7]

Published work is mainly retrospective series and case reports. The 85-patient series above reports complication rates.[1] A prospective study of 20 patients with surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion, an alternative way to widen the upper jaw, found mean maximum expansion at the first molar of 7.48 mm with about 30% dental relapse during later orthodontics.[8] Registered trials include one comparing one-piece with segmental Le Fort I osteotomy in cleft patients (n=60) and another comparing segmental osteotomy with surgically assisted expansion for transverse maxillary deficiency (n=90).[9][10]

timeline.event: René Le Fort describes the midface fracture patterns that name the Le Fort I level.[3]
British series reports complication rates of segmental Le Fort I osteotomy.[1]
